source.title: Predictable Scale: Part II, Farseer: A Refined Scaling Law in Large Language Models
source.authors: Houyi Li; Wen-Zheng Zheng; Qiu-Feng Wang; Zhenyu Ding; Haoying Wang; Zi-Li Wang; Shijie Xuyang; Ning Ding; Shuigeng Zhou; Xiangyu Zhang; Da-Xin Jiang

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some figure labels are garbled in the text extraction, but the main text and appendices are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out loss across model and data scales, compares its fitted law with Chinchilla’s, and argues that loss interactions and fitting choices require a refined formulation.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper’s own held-out BPC scaling fits, extrapolation tests, compute-allocation analysis, architecture-shape experiments, parameter-counting ablation, and fitting-method comparison. Cited results about downstream tasks and recent models are not recorded as study results.
record.test_reason: The authors train about 1,000 Llama-style models and measure held-out BPC across N and D. They show the additive Chinchilla power law misfits systematically and argue for a refined surface with N-dependent data exponents. They test extrapolation up to 25.1B, derive compute-optimal D/N, ablate model shape, and vary parameter counting and fitting method. These results bear directly on V1, V2, V3, V4 and V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors further claim Farseer is more fundamental than Chinchilla's law. They argue Chinchilla's additive form misses N–D interaction, fitting only mid-range N. They also say Chinchilla's D/N of about 20 underestimates data needs at larger budgets, and that excluding embedding parameters gives better extrapolation.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes a differential piecewise fitting method and a refined loss surface rather than reproducing the original Kaplan or Hoffmann fitting recipes; it compares against Chinchilla and also tests standard non-linear regression.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes depend on fitting method (standard regression versus differential piecewise fitting), whether embedding parameters are included in N, fitting-data volume, and training-data recipe (Baseline versus EN-ZH).

fits_no_version.finding: Small-scale point and line comparisons between 85% and 50% English data mixtures can reverse at larger N and D on the fitted surface (Appendix E, Fig 15).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Rankings of training recipes made at small scale can reverse at larger scale.

record.peer_reviewed: Neural Information Processing Systems (2025); the paper text identifies itself as a preprint under review.
record.problems: The authors restrict experiments to Llama-style decoder-only Transformers and two pretraining data distributions; validation reaches 25.1 B parameters but not larger scales. The paper reports no uncertainty intervals for the headline prediction errors, gives no theoretical derivation, and explicitly leaves other architecture families and modalities unexplored. Downstream task performance is not evaluated.

untested.parts: There is no power law in compute. The N-direction law is not shown as a power law; a stretched exponential fits better. The non-bottleneck conditions are not separately tested.
Nothing beyond 25.1B, which is about 4x the largest fitted N. No extrapolation spans several orders of magnitude in N.
There are no IsoFLOP-measured optima and no separate exponents for N_opt and D_opt. The stability of the allocation exponents is not checked.
Only aspect ratio and FFN ratio are varied. Attention type, norm placement and activation function are not.
All parts: other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer.
All parts: no downstream tasks are evaluated.
Training schedule is not varied. Whether exponents differ across data recipes is not reported.

missing.what: Functional form comparison for E+U(N): power law gives relative error 0.0083 versus 0.0011 for a stretched exponential. A power law in N is a worse fit.
Functional form comparison for A(N) and B(N): power-law+power-law 0.1322 versus stretched-exp+stretched-exp 0.1125.
R² values for finite-difference power laws along other directions: 0.7457, 0.8484 and 0.8733.
The D exponent A(N) varies over about 0.25–0.40 across model sizes.
Chinchilla versus Farseer extrapolation error at 6.4B and 25.1B as the fitting upper bound grows. Chinchilla error remains persistently high.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The authors' claim that 25.1B is more than an order of magnitude beyond calibration does not hold in N (6.37B to 25.1B is about 4x). No uncertainty intervals are reported. The V1 verdict was moved from challenges to limits_scope: loss still falls predictably and the data term is a power law in D, but the N term and the joint form depart from a simple power law.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports held-out BPC fits over model and data sizes, but does not separately establish a power law in compute or test the stated non-bottleneck conditions in the Kaplan formulation.
Extrapolation is tested on the reported model family and data recipes, with validation up to 25.1 B parameters; larger-scale predictions are not validated.

The paper reports an increasing optimal D/N trend with compute, but does not report fitted power exponents for optimal parameter count and token count separately or test whether they grow equally or at different rates.
The shape experiments cover aspect ratio and FFN ratio, not every architectural detail or a wide range of architecture families.
Other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer are not tested; the paper explicitly leaves multimodal and diffusion settings unexplored.
The study evaluates held-out BPC, not downstream task performance or its predictability from pretraining loss.

The paper tests selected fitting methods, parameter-counting conventions, and two data recipes, but does not systematically vary all listed setup factors or independently establish the generality of its fitted exponents.

rows.subject: Farseer and Chinchilla fits on the study’s Llama-style decoder-only Transformer models (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Baseline models range from 2.01 × 10^8 to 6.37 × 10^9 non-embedding parameters; training data range is roughly 1.00 × 10^9 to 5.12 × 10^11 tokens.
rows.operation_detail: Fit and compare loss surfaces against empirical held-out BPC values.

conditions.value: Farseer differential piecewise fitting; Chinchilla standard non-linear regression

rows.measure: Average relative error / fit to empirical BPC
rows.value: Farseer’s error is reported as 232% lower within the fitted range; Chinchilla systematically underestimates at low D and overestimates at high D.
rows.note: Aggregate comparison. The paper attributes the difference to Farseer’s model-size-dependent data-scaling coefficients and exponents; the reported result supports a refined loss surface rather than a single simple law.
rows.check: For V1, loss falls smoothly, but the additive Chinchilla power law under-predicts at low D and over-predicts at high D. Its error diverges at extreme N. For V7 this is fully observed: the functional form changes the fit (Farseer error 232% lower). Treat as partial for V1 and observed for V7.

source_check.correct: Split states by version: V1 partial; V7 observed. The functional-form comparison directly demonstrates fit dependence.
source_check.problem: The shared partial state understates the observed V7 effect.

rows.subject: Farseer-trained Llama-style decoder-only Transformer models (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Extrapolation targets include a 25.1 B model; the largest baseline model used in fitting is 6.37 × 10^9 parameters.
rows.operation_detail: Fit on a 2-spaced grid of smaller model and dataset sizes, then predict six larger or off-grid targets.

conditions.value: Six extrapolation targets, including larger datasets and off-grid (N, D) combinations

rows.measure: Average relative error across extrapolation targets
rows.note: Aggregate across the six reported validation targets.
rows.check: Observed for both. The Chinchilla baseline (2.68% average error) is itself a V2 power-law extrapolation that does markedly worse than Farseer, so the row also shows the V7 form-dependence.

source_check.correct: Sampling-grid spacing: √2. Farseer average relative error: 0.50%; Chinchilla: 2.68%. V7 observed; distinguish Farseer's refined-form extrapolation from the narrower V2 evidence supplied by the Chinchilla comparison.
source_check.problem: The grid spacing omits √; accurate extrapolation of Farseer's non-power-law model-size form does not itself establish V2.

rows.subject: Farseer-trained 25.1 B Llama-style decoder-only Transformer model
rows.operation_detail: Predict BPC at a model scale beyond the fitting range.
rows.note: The authors describe this target as extending the evaluation domain beyond the largest calibrated scale by more than an order of magnitude.
rows.check: Remove V7: a single Farseer error says nothing about fit-dependence. The authors describe 25.1B as more than an order of magnitude beyond calibration. In N it is only about 4x the largest fitted model (6.37B), so the gap holds only in compute, if at all.

source_check.correct: Relative error: 0.47% at 25.1B. V2 state: cannot_determine from this Farseer-only result. The fitted model-size dependence is stretched exponential; the largest Baseline fitting model is 6.37B.
source_check.problem: The result demonstrates refined-form extrapolation, rather than the power-law extrapolation specified by V2.

rows.subject: Farseer-trained 6.4 B Llama-style decoder-only Transformer models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Fit on subsets with progressively larger upper bounds and predict the excluded 6.4 B models.
rows.note: The paper reports that error decreases nearly monotonically as more model-size points are included.
rows.check: A 0.6% error predicting 6.4B from models up to 1.9B is accurate, so the state is observed, not partial. The scale gap is about 3x, not orders of magnitude. Remove V7: fitting-data volume is not one of the listed setup choices.

source_check.correct: Relative error: 6.01 × 10^-3 when fitting through 1.9B and predicting excluded 6.4B models. V2 state: cannot_determine from this Farseer-only result.
source_check.problem: The numerical result is accurate, but the extrapolated model-size dependence is not a power law.

rows.subject: Farseer-trained EN-ZH Llama-style decoder-only Transformer models (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Excluded target models are 3.2 B parameters
rows.operation_detail: Fit using progressively more EN-ZH models and predict deliberately excluded 3.2 B models.
rows.note: Aggregate reported for the EN-ZH recipe; the paper says error steadily converges as fitting data increases.
rows.check: Remove V7. The paper does not report whether fitted exponents differ between the EN-ZH and Baseline recipes. The target (3.2B) is close to the largest fitted EN-ZH model.

source_check.problem: Generalization of the refined functional form does not directly establish power-law extrapolation.

rows.subject: Farseer loss surface fitted to the study’s Llama-style decoder-only Transformer models
rows.operation_detail: Minimize fitted loss over parameter and data allocation at a fixed compute budget C = 6ND.
rows.measure: Optimal D/N ratio as compute budget changes
rows.value: Farseer predicts a steadily increasing optimal D/N ratio as compute budget grows.
rows.note: The paper reports a trend, but does not provide fitted power exponents for optimal N and D separately.
rows.check: Optimal D/N is derived from the fitted surface under C=6ND, not measured with IsoFLOP runs. For V3 it departs from Hoffmann's constant ratio, since D grows faster than N. No separate exponents are given, so stability cannot be checked. For V7 it is observed: the Chinchilla and Farseer laws give different splits.

source_check.correct: Split states by version: V3 partial; V7 observed. Under C = 6ND, the fitted Farseer surface predicts increasing optimal D/N; the Chinchilla comparison is around 20, typically 10–30. Separate stable allocation exponents are not reported.
source_check.problem: The shared partial state understates the observed dependence of allocation guidance on functional form.

rows.subject: Chinchilla loss law
rows.operation_detail: Compare its compute-optimal token-to-parameter guidance with Farseer’s.
rows.value: Around 20, typically 10–30; the paper says this underestimates requirements at larger scale.
rows.note: This is the paper’s described Chinchilla guidance, compared with its own Farseer allocation result.
rows.check: This is the described Chinchilla rule of thumb (D/N about 20), used as the comparator for R7, not a separate study result. It should be merged into R7's baseline.

rows.size_stated: Fixed parameter count; exact count not stated
rows.operation_detail: Vary aspect ratio (hidden dimension / layer count) while holding parameter count or estimated compute approximately constant.
rows.value: The curve is described as having a broad, flat optimum; reference levels shown are +0.5% at 0.5293 and +1% at 0.5320.
rows.note: The text explicitly describes a relatively flat optimum. Individual curve values are not given in the extracted text.
rows.check: The figure caption gives no parameter count. The aspect ratio range on the x-axis runs to about 500.

rows.size_stated: Fixed parameter count; exact count not stated
rows.operation_detail: Vary FFN ratio (intermediate size / hidden dimension) while holding parameter count or estimated compute approximately constant.
rows.value: The curve is described as having a broad, flat optimum; reference levels shown are +0.5% at 0.5293 and +1% at 0.5320.
rows.note: The text explicitly describes a relatively flat optimum. Individual curve values are not given in the extracted text.
rows.check: The FFN ratio range on the x-axis runs to about 5000%. The parameter count is unstated.

rows.subject: Farseer fit using non-embedding parameter count
rows.operation_detail: Fit a scaling law with model size excluding embedding parameters and evaluate at 25.1 B.
rows.baseline: Fit including embedding parameters has error 0.029
rows.value: More than four times smaller error than the fit including embedding parameters.
rows.note: The paper does not state the exact error for the non-embedding fit in the text.
rows.check: Pair with R12. Excluding embeddings gives an error more than 4x smaller at 25.1B.

rows.subject: Farseer fit using total parameter count including embeddings
rows.operation_detail: Fit a scaling law with embedding parameters included in model size and evaluate at 25.1 B.
rows.note: The authors report substantially worse extrapolation than when embeddings are excluded.
rows.check: The state should be observed: the counting choice changes 25.1B extrapolation error to 0.029, which is the V7 effect. Both counting conventions fit equally well locally.

rows.subject: Farseer loss model
rows.operation_detail: Compare standard end-to-end non-linear regression with differential piecewise fitting.
rows.value: Standard regression errors are approximately 10 times higher than those from differential piecewise fitting.
rows.note: The paper reports that extensive initialization did not make standard regression converge to an optimal global solution for Farseer.
rows.check: An order-of-magnitude error difference between fitting methods fully shows fitting-method dependence for the Farseer form.

rows.subject: Chinchilla loss model
rows.operation_detail: Compare standard non-linear regression with differential piecewise fitting.
rows.value: Standard non-linear regression yields a marginally better fit.
rows.note: The text does not quantify the difference.
rows.check: For Chinchilla, the two fitting methods differ only marginally. The difference is unquantified in the text, though Fig 17a carries values.

rows.subject: Llama-style decoder-only Transformer models in the study (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Model sizes span the ranges in the Baseline and EN-ZH experiments
rows.operation_detail: Analyze the finite difference in held-out loss as training data size changes at fixed model size.
rows.measure: Power-law fit of loss difference against D
rows.value: Average R² = 0.9807; the paper reports a power-law relationship across studied model sizes.
rows.note: This is a power law for the finite difference in loss, not a direct test that the full loss itself follows one fixed power law.
rows.check: Add V1: at fixed N, the data-dependent loss difference follows a power law in D (R²=0.9807). Its exponent A(N) varies with N (Fig 4), which is V7-relevant. The finite-difference power law has lower R² against N (0.7457–0.8733, Fig 3b–d), and those values are not recorded.
